content:
Local weather is one of the most underrated variables in Apple Home automation. Over the past few years, I have used sensors for all kinds of applications, whether it is reminding me to let the faucet drip in freezing weather, or adjusting the sprinkler schedule via Eve Aqua on hot days. The Eve Weather has been part of my setup for some time, and since it gained Matter support a few years ago, it has worked wonderfully in my home.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips, and everything related to the Apple smart home framework.

If you have been reading HomeKit Weekly for a while, you will know how much I love automation setups that can run on their own. Smart home accessories are only truly useful when they can perform certain actions automatically. That is exactly why I have always recommended building your smart home around a single ecosystem, rather than mixing and matching. Even in the Matter era, I have no desire to juggle a bunch of different platforms. For me, that platform is Apple Home. I prefer Eve devices because they have always taken privacy seriously, and as long as you stick with Matter-supported local control, you can skip the cloud account requirement. Eve has also been actively supporting Matter and Thread in recent years. This is exactly what everyone wants to see.

The Eve Weather delivers three readings from a single small device: temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure. It carries an IPX4 water resistance rating, and its aluminium body means it looks right at home outside my house. My unit is mounted outdoors. It provides highly localised readings that often differ by a few degrees from what the Apple Weather app shows. Honestly, that gap matters enormously when it is extremely hot or cold. When your pipes freeze at 31 degrees Fahrenheit and your app shows 34, you will certainly regret not having local data.

One of the Eve Weather's underrated features is its built-in 12-hour weather trend display. It uses barometric pressure changes to forecast how the weather is going to develop, and you can see a visual icon showing whether it will be sunny, cloudy, rainy, or stormy. This small touch adds a lot of practical value, letting you take it in at a glance without having to open an app on your phone.

Here are a few automations you can build with the Eve Weather:

  • When the temperature drops below freezing, turn on a coloured light to remind the family to let the faucets drip.
  • When outdoor humidity is particularly high, switch on the dehumidifier.
  • If it has already rained and the forecast shows more on the way, delay the sprinkler system from kicking in.
  • Ask Siri for the current front yard temperature without stepping outside.

Matter and Thread support in 2026

A few years ago, Eve released a free firmware update that brought Matter support to the Eve Weather. If you already own the device, you can upgrade it through the Eve app. The Matter version supports Apple Home, as well as Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings. The sensor itself is identical; it simply becomes cross-platform, which makes things much easier if you ever want to switch to a different smart home ecosystem in the future.

The Eve Weather is what is known as a Minimal Thread Device. That means it communicates over Thread, but does not relay traffic. That job is handled by Full Thread Devices that run around the clock, such as the Eve Energy or Eve Water Guard. The more Full Thread Devices you have, the stronger and more reliable your Thread network becomes, and battery-powered devices like the Eve Weather benefit directly from that stability.

You still do not need an Eve account. Unless you opt in yourself, all data stays local. The Eve iPhone app is an excellent tool for visualising and tracking historical temperature, barometric pressure, and humidity trends. It is a really interesting way to spot patterns and make smarter decisions around things like lawn irrigation and energy management.

I have a few HomePod minis placed around the house, and I rely on an Eero 6E network to back Thread. The Eero system has Thread support built into the software, so it provides a solid foundation for accessories like the Eve Weather, keeping the connection stable and responsive.

Eve Weather wrap-up

The only thing I would still like to see is a rechargeable battery. The current battery can last for several months, but I would prefer a USB-C port like the one on the Eve Room. That said, the Eve Weather remains one of my favourite Apple Home accessories. It is minimalist, looks great, and performs well across all the major platforms thanks to Matter. If you want to bring local weather data into your smart home and trigger practical automations, the Eve Weather is an easy recommendation from me.

You can buy it directly from Amazon or from the Eve website.
